items.followUp: Give four differences between an element and a compound.

rubric.why: Shows that compounds have a fixed composition while mixtures can have a variable composition.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the correct contrast in composition.

rubric.why: Distinguishes chemical combination in a compound from physical mixing in a mixture.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct contrast in how the substances are combined.

rubric.why: Recognises that a compound has properties different from its elements, whereas mixture components retain their properties.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct contrast in component properties.

rubric.why: Identifies the different ways compounds and mixtures are separated.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that compounds require chemical methods to separate, while mixtures can be separated physically.

modelAnswer: A compound has a fixed composition, whereas a mixture can have a variable composition.
The elements in a compound are chemically combined, whereas substances in a mixture are physically mixed.
The properties of a compound differ from those of its constituent elements, whereas mixture components retain their properties.
The elements of a compound can be separated by chemical methods, whereas mixture components can be separated by physical methods.

items.followUp: Write down any five properties of non-metals.

rubric.why: Lustre is a characteristic physical property of most metals.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that metals are lustrous or shiny.

rubric.why: Metals can generally be hammered or rolled into sheets.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying malleability.

rubric.why: Metals can generally be drawn into wires.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying ductility.

rubric.why: Metals are generally good conductors of heat and electricity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that metals conduct heat or electricity well.

rubric.why: Metals produce a ringing sound when struck.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying sonority.

modelAnswer: Metals are generally lustrous (shiny).
Metals are malleable and can be hammered into sheets.
Metals are ductile and can be drawn into wires.
Metals are good conductors of heat and electricity.
Metals are sonorous and produce a ringing sound when struck.

items.followUp: Define boiling and state two factors that affect the boiling point of a liquid.

rubric.why: Defines evaporation as the change of a liquid into vapour from its surface.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the change of liquid to vapour at the surface.

rubric.why: Increasing temperature increases the rate of evaporation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying temperature as a factor.

rubric.why: A larger exposed surface allows more molecules to escape per unit time.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying exposed surface area as a factor.

rubric.why: Humidity and air movement affect how readily vapour leaves the liquid's surroundings.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying humidity or wind speed/air movement as a factor.

modelAnswer: Evaporation is the change of a liquid into vapour from its surface at a temperature below its boiling point.
The rate of evaporation increases with an increase in temperature.
The rate of evaporation increases with an increase in the surface area exposed to air.
The rate of evaporation increases with increased wind speed and decreases with increased humidity.

items.followUp: Define an alloy and describe three methods used to protect iron from rusting.

rubric.why: Corrosion is the gradual deterioration of a metal through chemical reaction with its environment.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining corrosion as the gradual chemical deterioration of a metal.

rubric.why: Rusting is the corrosion of iron in the presence of oxygen and moisture, forming rust.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking iron, oxygen and moisture to rust formation.

rubric.why: Paint forms a barrier that keeps air and moisture away from the metal.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming painting or another valid method of preventing corrosion.

rubric.why: Several other methods prevent the metal from contacting corrosive substances or protect it electrochemically.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a second distinct valid method.

rubric.why: A third distinct method demonstrates knowledge of corrosion prevention.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a third distinct valid method.

modelAnswer: Corrosion is the gradual destruction of a metal by chemical reaction with substances in its environment.
Rusting is the corrosion of iron in the presence of oxygen and moisture, forming hydrated iron oxide (rust).
Painting the iron surface prevents air and moisture from reaching it.
Oiling or greasing forms a protective layer on the iron.
Galvanizing coats iron with zinc to protect it from corrosion.

items.followUp: State four differences between a true solution and a colloid.

rubric.why: A colloid is a heterogeneous mixture, even though it may appear uniform.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a colloid is heterogeneous.

rubric.why: Colloidal particles scatter a beam of light, producing the Tyndall effect.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying light scattering or the Tyndall effect.

rubric.why: Colloidal particles remain dispersed and do not settle on standing.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the particles do not settle on standing.

accept: cannot be separated by ordinary filtration
rubric.why: Colloidal particles pass through ordinary filter paper, so ordinary filtration does not separate them.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly describing their behaviour during ordinary filtration.

modelAnswer: A colloid is a heterogeneous mixture, although it may appear homogeneous.
Colloidal particles scatter light; this is called the Tyndall effect.
The particles remain dispersed and do not settle on standing.
Colloidal particles pass through ordinary filter paper and cannot be separated by ordinary filtration.

items.followUp: Define chemical properties and give two examples.

rubric.why: A physical property can be observed or measured without changing the substance's chemical identity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining a physical property as one observed or measured without a chemical change.

rubric.why: These are valid examples of physical properties.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving any two valid examples.

modelAnswer: Physical properties are properties that can be observed or measured without changing the chemical identity of a substance.
Examples include colour and density.

items.followUp: Define a mixture and give one example.

rubric.why: A compound consists of two or more elements chemically combined in a fixed proportion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a compound contains elements chemically combined in a fixed proportion.

rubric.why: Water, sodium chloride and carbon dioxide are valid examples of compounds.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct example.

modelAnswer: A compound is a pure substance formed when two or more elements are chemically combined in a fixed proportion.
Water (H₂O) is an example of a compound.

items.followUp: State one observation that Rutherford's gold-foil experiment could not explain using the Plum Pudding Theory.

rubric.why: The theory proposed that the atom was a sphere of positive charge.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the atom as a positively charged sphere.

rubric.why: The theory placed electrons within the positively charged sphere, like plums in a pudding.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that electrons are embedded or distributed within the positive sphere.

modelAnswer: The Plum Pudding Theory, proposed by J. J. Thomson, described the atom as a sphere of positive charge.
Electrons were embedded throughout this sphere, like plums in a pudding; the equal positive and negative charges made the atom neutral.
